parent.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Three Knights Variation
parent.moves: 1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 e6 3. Nf3 d5 4. Nc3
parent.overview: After 4.Nc3 (reached from 3.Nf3 or 3.Nc3) both sides have developed two pieces and the centre is still in tension; neither has committed. White keeps a choice of 5.Bg5 (the classical Orthodox set-ups), 5.cxd5 (Exchange structures with a Carlsbad pawn structure), 5.e3 (quieter) or Bf4, and Black's 4th move (...Be7, ...Bb4 Ragozin, ...Nbd7 Cambridge Springs set-up) picks the structure. In the main Orthodox lines White pins or pressures the f6 knight and tries to exploit Black's passive light-squared bishop behind e6; Black aims to complete development, castle, and free the position with ...c5, ...e5 or ...dxc4 plus ...b6/...Bb7. The game is usually slow and manoeuvring with the d4/d5 pawns holding the centre; wins come from small structural or space edges rather than early tactics. At 2500 level draws spike (11.7 percent in the Chessiverse data), and it is regarded as one of Black's most reliable replies to 1.d4.

parent.name: Center Game Accepted
parent.overview: The root is the crossroads after 2.d4 exd4, with Black a pawn up and White to move. White's main choice is 3.Qxd4 Nc6 4.Qe3 (Paulsen Attack): the pawn is regained, Black gains a tempo on the queen, and White castles queenside after Nc3 and Bd2, using the queen on e3 and the d-file to aim at g7 and the kingside. Black has calm, sound ways to equalise (4...Nf6, 4...Be7 preparing ...d5, 4...g6, 4...Bb4+) and can counterattack White's king on the queenside. The alternative 3.c3 is the Danish Gambit, where White gives one or two pawns for open lines and development. 3.Nf3 or 3.Bc4 lead to Scotch, Scotch Gambit, Petroff-type or Urusov positions. Overall it is old and rarely played at the top level, though with a modern revival (Shabalov, then Nepomniachtchi and Erigaisi, Shirov, Adams) as a practical, objectively equal surprise.

parent.name: Hungarian Opening
parent.overview: White plays 1.g3 to fianchetto the king's bishop to g2 and hit the long diagonal, deferring any central commitment (s1, s3). It is a flank opening that usually transposes: into the King's Indian Attack (Nf3, d3, O-O, then e4), the Catalan, the Réti or the English, depending on Black's set-up (s1, s3, s4). Black can happily occupy the centre with ...d5 or ...e5, or choose Sicilian, Caro-Kann or King's Indian-style set-ups (s2, s3). Positions are usually closed or flexible, with long-term strategic play rather than early tactics (s1, s3). Engines and statistics find it essentially equal, with White at most slightly more comfortable (s3, s4). Theory is minimal: it is closer to a move order than a distinct variation (s2).

parent.name: Italian Game: Giuoco Piano
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bc4 Bc5
parent.overview: Both sides develop the king's bishop to its active diagonal (Bc4 and ...Bc5), eyeing f7/f2. White's choice at move 4 decides the character. Slow lines are 4.c3 followed by d3 or d4 and the modern Giuoco Pianissimo with d3 (Re1, Nbd2-f1-g3, a4, h3): White postpones any central clash and the game is a patient manoeuvring battle. The sharper lines are the classical 4.c3 Nf6 5.d4 (Greco's Attack, Moller Attack), where White sacrifices a pawn for initiative, and the Evans Gambit 4.b4, a pawn for rapid development and an attack on f7. The Three Knights 4.Nc3 and 4.O-O are also main subtree moves. Black mirrors development, challenges the centre with ...d5, and has sufficient defensive resources. It is a respected choice used by Karpov and, as a Ruy Lopez sidestep, by Carlsen.

parent.name: Polish Opening
parent.overview: White plays 1.b4 to grab queenside space and fianchetto the bishop to b2, putting long-diagonal pressure on e5, f6 and g7. It is an irregular flank opening: Black chooses the set-up with 1...e5 (2.Bb2 Bxb4 3.Bxe5, the Exchange Variation, which equalises), 1...d5 (the German Defence 2...Qd6 etc.), or 1...Nf6 and 1...e6 reaching Indian-like or Queen's Gambit-like set-ups. The opening is sound and not refuted but gives Black no real problems, so it is rarely seen at elite level and chosen as a surprise weapon (Carlsen used it against Nakamura and So in 2021). Theory is small and the play is flank-oriented, with unbalanced pawn structures but typically no early forced tactics. Alekhine's complaint was that it reveals White's intentions before knowing Black's.

parent.name: Philidor Defense
parent.overview: Black defends e5 with the d-pawn instead of the knight, building a compact centre at the cost of space and piece mobility. Wikipedia calls it solid but passive (s1); the dark-squared bishop and sometimes the whole position can be cramped (s2, s4). The usual game is White taking space after 3.d4 or developing with 3.Bc4, and Black setting up the Hanham formation (...Nf6, ...Nbd7, ...Be7, ...c6, ...O-O), then freeing the position by ...exd4 or ...d5 at the right moment (s1, s4). Modern analysis finds it dynamically balanced, not just passive (s3). Strong players use it rarely; Wikipedia says no top player used it regularly as of 2017, though it has grown in rapid, blitz and bullet (s1). Move orders matter: Black must avoid several tactical pitfalls (s2, s4).

parent.name: Petrov's Defense
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nf6 3. Nxe5 d6
parent.overview: Black answers 2.Nf3 by counter-attacking e4 rather than defending e5. After 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.d4 d5 6.Bd3 both sides have lost an e-pawn and the structure is symmetrical, with the e-file the main open line. Black's aim is to equalise by quick development and piece trades; White tries to turn a small lead in development or slightly freer play into pressure, often castling and using the e-file or a queenside castling and pawn storm. The 3.d4 Steinitz line (3...Nxe4 4.Bd3 d5 5.Nxe5 Nd7) and 3.Nc3 (Four Knights transposition) or 3.d3 sidelines give quieter or more varied structures. The main lines are widely played at the top and are known as drawish, though some lines hold real attacking chances for both sides.

parent.name: King's Indian Defense: Normal Variation
parent.moves: 1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 g6 3. Nc3 Bg7 4. e4 d6 5. Be2
parent.overview: This root is the King's Indian reached by the move order 1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.c4 (the same position as 3.Nf3 in the 2.c4 move order). It is not a distinct opening: it is the ordinary King's Indian, where Black fianchettoes with ...Bg7, castles, and strikes at White's centre with ...e5, ...c5 or ...f5. White's choice of set-up decides the character: the classical 4.Nc3 and e4 leads to the locked-centre opposite-wing race (c4-c5 against ...f5-f4), while the Fianchetto Variation (g3, Bg2, O-O, Nc3) is quieter, positional, and has less forcing theory. The data subtree groups 4.e4 Normal Variation lines (the majority of games) under this root, so it mixes both. Black's success depends on timing and coordination rather than automatic aggression.

parent.name: Sicilian Defense: French Variation
parent.moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 e6 3. d4 cxd4
parent.overview: 2...e6 is a gateway rather than a set-up: after 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Black chooses the Taimanov (...Nc6), the Kan (...a6) or the Scheveningen (...d6, ...Nf6), with 3.Nc3 giving the Paulsen/Kan/Taimanov move orders. Black opens the diagonal for the f8-bishop and prepares ...d5 or ...Nc6/...a6 in a flexible way, with a solid ...e6/...d6 pawn chain and queenside counterplay. The name 'French' is only a naming convention: the pawn structure is Sicilian, not a French one. White's main choice is 3.d4 (about 61% of moves at 2500); rarer third moves are 3.d3, 3.g3, 3.c3 and Westerinen's 3.b3 (Bb2, occasional in the 1970s). At higher levels play is heavily theoretical.
